question.text: Scenario: Meera (age 48) was recently widowed after her husband's sudden demise. She has received an insurance payout of Rs. 1,50,00,000 (Rs. 1.5 crore). She receives a pension of Rs. 35,000 per month from her late husband's employer. Meera has two children — the elder child (age 20) is currently in college, and the younger child (age 16) will need higher education funding in 2 years. Meera owns her house outright with no outstanding loan. Her existing investments include: Rs. 25,00,000 in equity mutual funds, Rs. 10,00,000 in fixed deposits, and Rs. 5,00,000 in physical gold. Before her husband's death, the couple had been jointly assessed as having an Aggressive risk profile. Meera's monthly household expenses are Rs. 65,000. She approaches her investment adviser Anand for guidance on managing the insurance corpus and restructuring her portfolio. Question 2 of 5: When reassessing Meera's risk profile, which combination of factors would Anand need to consider MOST carefully?

answer.text: Only her total asset value, since it has increased significantly with the insurance payout

Her pension income of Rs. 35,000/month against expenses of Rs. 65,000/month, two dependents with education time frames, and her household assets and liabilities including ability and willingness to absorb losses
Only the performance of her existing equity mutual fund portfolio
Only her age and the number of years to retirement

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook lists the factors that risk profiling should consider: age, investment objectives, time frames, resources such as income and existing investments, innate willingness and ability to take risk, ability to absorb losses, and loans. For Meera, this means weighing pension income against expenses (a Rs. 30,000 monthly gap), the time frames for two dependents needing education funding, her assets and the absence of liabilities (she owns the house outright), and her overall ability and willingness to absorb losses. The Trap: Options A, C and D each isolate a single factor; the source explicitly contemplates a combined assessment across several inputs. Having a large lump sum does not by itself sustain an aggressive profile when the regular income stream is much smaller than expenses. Note: Emotional state is real adviser context after bereavement but is not one of the source's listed risk-profiling factors; the keyed option avoids relying on it as a SEBI Regulation 16 requirement.
